title: Assembling the USO band; Charles returns from the Navy
summary: Two sidemen fail the physical, he hires replacements in New York including bassist Carl Pruitt, and Charles, just discharged, rejoins in November 1945.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: But we got processed for this trip. Then I found I had two men in the band who couldn't pass the examination. One was Bill Martin. He had a heart murmur. And the other was Amos Woodruff, who had a bad ticker, and he was fat and a little bit overweight. So they sent them back to St. Louis.
I looked around New York, trying to get some musicians. I found a couple of young musicians who had been hanging out

with Dizzy. I asked them, did they want a job. One of them told me, "Well, Pops, I'll have to hear the band first. I might not dig it," you know. I said, "Well, that's quite all right, son. Don't worry about it." So I got on the phone, called back to St. Louis, and got Crack Stanley down there; we needed a trombone player. We got a Story on the trombone. And there's a boy named Sam up there I ran into, seemed like he was a nice fellow, and I'd heard he was a nice trumpet player. So we hired him.

So there was a boy named Carl Pruitt, an excellent bass player. I mean, a top calibre bass player, Carl Pruitt. We hired him. And we had a little saxophone player named Rudy. Rudy was quite popular at the Savoy Ballroom, and he was from New Jersey. And the day we got ready to leave, Rudy showed up high, and just almost drunk. So we decided to leave Rudy in New York, and we left without another saxophonist, and that was when they sent us Levy, wasn't it? You remember Levy?
Uh-huh. How'd I get in there?
Huh?
How'd I get in there?
I called you and told you that if you wanted to make this deal you better come on up here and get it. And you got in town just a few days before we left.
Got in there the 16th -- fourth of November, wasn't it?
Huh? Yes.
Oh, that's right. I heard from Julie sent me a night letter, because I was going to stay in Chicago.
Yeah, that's right. My wife sent him a night letter, see.
Now, what year was this?
That was 1945.
'45. And you were out of the Navy.
Uh-huh.
He was out of the Navy--
I got discharged on the 30th of September, in '45. And I was going to stay on in Chicago.

He was gonna stay on in Chicago. And I had this good deal -- a year's work, see. Almost a year's work, see. And so I had my wife send him a telegram, see. And so he came back, he came at breakneck speed, see, and he just came to town. in time.
So we had Charles, my brother, Charles, and they sent us a baritone saxophone player. And he arrived in Manila after we got there. So we left on this special train.
